text.en: Belgium and Sri Lanka both have people who speak different languages. One shared power and stayed together; the other did not, and went through a long civil conflict. Today we learn why.

In Belgium about 59 per cent of people live in the Dutch-speaking region and about 40 per cent in the French-speaking region, with a small German-speaking community. Brussels is a mixed capital.
The Belgians changed the Constitution to share power: equal Dutch and French ministers in the central government, state governments with powers of their own, and a separate Community Government for each language group.
In Sri Lanka, Sinhala-speakers are about 74 per cent and Tamil-speakers about 18 per cent. In 1956 an Act made Sinhala the only official language.
The majoritarian measures made Tamils feel alienated, and the conflict grew into a civil war.
Power sharing is good because it reduces conflict between groups and is the very spirit of democracy, as it gives people a say.
Forms of power sharing include horizontal sharing among legislature, executive and judiciary, vertical sharing among levels of government, sharing among social groups, and sharing among parties and movements.
Horizontal sharing is also called a system of checks and balances.
Community government in Belgium and reserved constituencies in India are examples of sharing power among social groups.

problem.en: In Belgium 59 per cent speak Dutch and 40 per cent French. What per cent is left?

prompt.en: Explain why power sharing is desirable.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking majority rule means no sharing

points.en: Belgium shared power and Sri Lanka did not.
There are four forms of power sharing.
Power sharing is the spirit of democracy.
